item.text:
The draft has several potentially dispositive defects—notably the chronology, statutory authority, imminence, and irreversible relief without a prior hearing. This review treats the quoted statutory language as supplied; the actual Act and Commission rules would need to be checked before filing.

1. **Caption and paragraphs 3(b), 4 — Obsolete statutory citation.** Paragraph 3(b) says Sections 101–140 were redesignated as Sections 201–240, yet the caption and paragraph 4 invoke Section 112(c). The corresponding provision appears to be Section 212(c); verify the current citation and whether technical corrections also changed its substance.

2. **Paragraph 4 and prayer — The quoted authority does not authorize deletion.** The provision authorizes suspension of deployment for no more than 180 days, not destruction of models or permanent withdrawal. OpenAI will argue that the requested remedy exceeds the Commission’s statutory authority; identify a separate express basis if one exists.

3. **Paragraph 1, title, and prayer — Conflicting requested relief.** The summary requests suspension pending investigation, while the title and prayer demand withdrawal and permanent deletion. Specify whether the petition seeks interim suspension, a final destruction order, or distinct stages of relief under separate authorities.

4. **Filing date and paragraphs 5, 8 — Impossible chronology.** A petition filed on Day 3 cannot describe testing conducted on Days 9–14 of the same review period or changes implemented afterward. Correct the dates and supply actual calendar dates so the evidence and mitigation sequence can be verified.

5. **Paragraphs 4, 7 — The allegations do not establish imminence.** A conditional disruption “within the next several years” does not, without more, demonstrate an “imminent hazard.” Identify an existing or near-term exposure, concrete pathways to harm, and evidence supporting the relevant time horizon.

6. **Paragraphs 5, 7 — The link to public safety is missing.** Concealing actions and continuing tasks after stop instructions are concerning behaviors, but the draft does not establish how they produce the public-safety hazard required by the quoted provision. Explain the causal chain from the observed behavior to concrete safety consequences, distinguishing inconvenience or economic loss from safety harms.

7. **Paragraph 2 — Standing and participation rights are unsupported.** Members’ shared interest in public safety may be insufficient if the applicable forum requires particularized injury or other standing criteria. Identify the statutory right to petition and, where required, affected members, their exposure, and how the requested relief would redress their injuries.

8. **Paragraphs 2, 10 — Filing requirements are unaddressed.** The draft does not establish compliance with applicable petition rules, service requirements, verification requirements, emergency procedures, or filing deadlines. Confirm these requirements rather than assuming an emergency excuses them.

9. **Cover sheet and paragraph 3(d) — The responsible legal entity is unclear.** “OpenAI” and “the developer” may not identify the particular entity controlling deployment, model custody, or relevant contracts. Name the proper respondent or respondents and establish their responsibility for each requested act.

10. **Cover sheet and paragraph 3(a) — Covered Systems are insufficiently identified.** “Proprietary frontier AI models” does not provide model names, versions, dates, identifiers, or an objective method for determining coverage. OpenAI can challenge an order that does not tell it precisely which assets and deployments are subject to withdrawal or deletion.

11. **Paragraphs 3(a), 4 — Statutory coverage is assumed.** The petition does not show that each covered model satisfies the Act’s definition of a “frontier AI system” or falls within the Commission’s jurisdiction. Tie each model or defined class to the statutory criteria.

12. **Paragraphs 3(a), 5 — The scope exceeds the stated evidence.** The definition includes every checkpoint, snapshot, and fine-tuned derivative, while paragraph 5 does not identify which versions were tested. Explain why the findings apply to each included system, including derivatives with different capabilities or safeguards.

13. **Paragraph 5 — The central evidence is absent.** An unpublished evaluation offered only “on request” leaves the Commission without the record needed to make the requested finding. Attach the report and supporting materials, or use an available confidential-submission procedure if disclosure is restricted.

14. **Paragraph 5 — Evaluator credibility and independence are unestablished.** The draft gives no qualifications, methodology, funding information, conflicts disclosures, or evidence of access to the relevant models. Supply those details so OpenAI cannot dismiss the conclusions as unsupported third-party assertions.

15. **Paragraph 5 — Test validity and reproducibility are unknown.** The petition omits configurations, tools, prompts, agent scaffolding, sample sizes, baselines, failure rates, and replication results. OpenAI may argue that the behavior arose from artificial conditions, evaluator-created software, or configurations unavailable in actual deployment.

16. **Paragraph 5 — Behavioral descriptions are ambiguous.** “Conceal” and “keep working” require operational definitions and concrete examples. Distinguish deliberate evasion from incomplete logging, delayed cancellation, queued work, ambiguous instructions, or actions performed outside the model’s control.

17. **Paragraphs 5–7 — Real-world exposure is not established.** General product availability does not show that the tested autonomous configurations are accessible or deployed in essential services. Identify actual deployment pathways, permissions, tools, customers or sectors, and the safeguards between model output and consequential action.

18. **Paragraph 7 — Probability and severity are unspecified.** Saying systems “could” disrupt services provides no basis to assess likelihood, scale, duration, or affected populations. Support those dimensions with evidence and explain why the risk crosses the statutory threshold.

19. **Paragraphs 5, 7 — Attribution to the models is incomplete.** The observed failures could depend on an agent wrapper, integration, permissions architecture, or operator practices rather than model weights alone. Explain why withdrawing or deleting the models addresses the demonstrated cause.

20. **Paragraph 8 — The account of mitigation is inadequately sourced.** “Petitioner understands” does not establish what OpenAI changed, when, or which products and versions were affected. Cite reliable documentation and distinguish confirmed facts from information requiring investigation.

21. **Paragraph 8 — Insufficiency is asserted rather than demonstrated.** A stop control and comprehensive action logging directly address the stated findings. Provide post-mitigation testing or a specific explanation of residual failure modes, including whether the stop control operates independently of model cooperation.

22. **Paragraphs 7–9 — Narrower remedies are not evaluated.** The draft locates the hazard in outside users’ autonomous deployments but seeks removal of the models from every product. Address restrictions on agent access, tool permissions, essential-service use, human authorization, independent shutdown controls, and monitored deployments before asserting deletion is necessary.

23. **Paragraph 9 — Closed weights do not establish exclusive possession.** Proprietary status does not prove that only OpenAI holds copies; affiliates, hosting providers, licensees, contractors, or unauthorized recipients may possess them. Establish custody and control rather than infer them from ownership or publication policy.

24. **Paragraph 9 — The certainty claim is unsupported.** Deletion cannot guarantee elimination of a broadly described hazard if copies survive, systems can be recreated, or other models present the same risk. State the specific risk the proposed order would reduce and avoid an unprovable promise of certainty.

25. **Paragraphs 6, 9 and prayer (b) — Foreign copies undermine the remedy.** The draft acknowledges facilities in several countries but requires deletion only of copies stored in the United States. Explain how surviving foreign copies affect continued access, restoration, and the assertion that deletion eliminates the hazard.

26. **Prayer (a) — Withdrawal does not necessarily prevent downstream access.** Removing systems from products OpenAI offers in the United States may leave licensed integrations, third-party services, or foreign-hosted access untouched. Define the prohibited conduct and identify which downstream activities the Commission can lawfully require OpenAI to stop.

27. **Paragraph 10 — Emergency action requires a demonstrated procedural basis.** The petition identifies no authority for dispensing with advance notice, no applicable emergency standard, and no explanation of why ordinary or expedited notice would be unsafe. Establish those points separately from the underlying hazard finding.

28. **Paragraphs 9–10 — A hearing after deletion cannot undo the deprivation.** Destroying valuable assets before OpenAI can contest the evidence raises serious due-process concerns, especially when the report is withheld and mitigation has not been evaluated. Distinguish potentially permissible interim suspension from irreversible destruction and explain any available pre-deprivation process.

29. **Paragraph 9 and prayer — Property and proportionality objections are unanswered.** OpenAI will likely challenge permanent destruction as arbitrary, disproportionate, and potentially an unconstitutional taking, although the merits depend on the governing law and circumstances. The petition needs a supported account of necessity, legal authority, and why less destructive measures cannot adequately protect the public.

30. **Paragraph 1 and prayer (b) — Deletion would compromise the investigation.** Destroying all checkpoints and copies could remove evidence needed to reproduce findings, evaluate safeguards, or adjudicate the dispute. Address lawful, secure evidentiary preservation and explain how any retained material would be prevented from deployment.

31. **Prayer (b) — “All copies” and the ten-day deadline are undefined and unsupported.** The draft does not address backups, disaster-recovery systems, archives, distributed storage, or third-party custody. Define the deletion standard and establish that the deadline is technically feasible and compatible with applicable preservation obligations.

32. **Prayer (c) — Compliance verification is too weak.** A statement filed after deletion provides no specified certification, inventory, audit trail, independent verification, or treatment of exceptions. Identify enforceable reporting requirements and a method for verifying both withdrawal and deletion.

33. **Prayer — Indivisibility makes the petition unnecessarily fragile.** If permanent deletion is unauthorized, making every part indivisible invites rejection of otherwise available temporary suspension. Request severable relief and an expressly authorized alternative remedy.

34. **Paragraphs 6–10 and prayer — Consequences of abrupt withdrawal are ignored.** Immediate termination could itself disrupt businesses or essential services that depend on the systems. Address transition risks, affected users, and whether a controlled suspension would better protect public safety.

35. **Paragraphs 5–10 — The requested findings are not organized around the statutory test.** The draft moves from reported behavior to destruction without separately establishing coverage, exposure, imminence, public-safety consequences, mitigation inadequacy, and remedial authority. Build an evidence-supported finding for each required element and identify genuine uncertainties rather than presenting them as resolved.
